title: An Easy Fix To Frequent Rule-Breaking
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers a structured six-step remedy for teachers who follow a classroom management plan consistently but are still frustrated by frequent rule-breaking, typically confined to just three to five recurring misbehaviors. His diagnosis is that these particular misbehaviors persist because they're either especially hard to resist or not yet deeply understood by students, meaning the fix isn't more consequences but more detail. The six steps are: identify the three to five recurring misbehaviors, understand why they persist, add detail (since detail always deepens understanding), model the exact misbehaviors as the teacher acting them out (which he calls the How-Not strategy), briefly explain why each is disruptive using the psychological research of Ellen Langer, and finally have student volunteers model both the misbehavior and the correct alternative. He stresses this only works as an add-on to a class that's already following through consistently -- otherwise it's a band-aid on a wound needing real surgery.
points: Most frequent rule-breaking traces back to just three to five specific recurring misbehaviors, not a general breakdown in class culture.
The 'How-Not strategy' has the teacher act out the actual misbehavior so students recognize themselves in the modeling.
The explanation of why a misbehavior is disruptive should stay brief, grounded in Ellen Langer's research on the power of explaining 'why.'
This detail-based fix only works as a supplement to a classroom management plan that's already being followed consistently.
quotes: If you follow a classroom management plan consistently but are still frustrated by how often rules are broken, there is an easy fix.
You’ll notice the same few misbehaviors are responsible for the high frequency of rule breaking. It’s usually between three and five.
The solution is more detail, even if the problem is confined to just a few students. Detail, no matter what you’re teaching, results in deeper understanding.
This is the key step. Model each of the misbehaviors you identified in step one. Act them out as if you’re one of your students.
The importance of ‘why’ is based on the research of psychologist Ellen Langer.
It’s worth repeating that the strategy only works—and your most challenging students will only care—if you’re already consistently following through.
